findings.reason: the census population must be the 43 acquisitions or 43 acquire/release pairs, otherwise the node writes 31 meaningless rows and the fragment's own count gate binds the wrong number.
findings.text: §4's gate is "row count equals the number of `fcntl.flock(` matches under `reckon/`", but that grep counts 74 call sites of which 31 pass `LOCK_UN` and only 43 acquire a lock (`reckon/project_state.py:315`, `reckon/_store.py:412`, `reckon/compliance.py:155`, …); a release site holds no lock, so its row can answer neither "what the lock guards" nor "whether a holder on another node can touch it", and the count the node must match is inflated by the releases

findings.reason: splitting the census (fragment only, no source writes) from a followup that migrates the rows it names gives each node one closeable verdict and a write scope the dispatch can declare.
findings.text: §4 delivers two things on one verdict, a read-only census fragment and the migration of "the modules of the rows the node moves to the §2 lock", and that second write scope is decided by the census rather than at dispatch, so the coordinator cannot fence the worker's paths when it enumerates "every row"

— §2's done-when prescribes the probe's launch as "`srun --partition=all_debug — from a shell where `SLURM_JOB_ID` is unset", a step sequence the harness contradicts: a worker on the fleet node runs inside a held allocation, where an `srun` executes as a step of that job whatever partition it names and only `sbatch` submits a job of its own, so the prescribed command does not reliably reach a second host. The plan's own "the two hostnames must differ" clause catches the failure, but only after a wasted round; WOULD_CHANGE_THE_PLAN: yes — REASON: stating the endpoint (a second invocation on a different node, hostnames printed and different) and leaving the launch to the node brief removes a method that the dispatch environment forbids.

— the cross-node probe bullet says the script "holds a plan-state resource lock through the production lock code" on a docs tree, and unlike the sibling test bullet (§2 bullet 4, "using a temporary docs tree") it never requires a temporary tree, so a worker following it will hold the production `flock(LOCK_EX)` on a live project's sprint resource — the blocking acquisition at `reckon/project_state.py:311` — for the probe's duration, stalling real plan writes on that resource while the base arm runs; WOULD_CHANGE_THE_PLAN: yes — REASON: one clause requiring a temporary docs tree, as the sibling bullet already has, removes a probe that can stall live sessions during its own negative control.

findings.reason: either declare `s3` depends-on `s2` (the followup's "§2 and §3 can run together" then becomes wrong too) or scope §3's claim to the injected faults, and the choice changes both the dependency graph and the dispatch order.
findings.text: §3's deliverable ends "An item never ends up in both sprints, or in neither", which is the production symptom §1 attributes to cross-node recovery and §2 exists to remove; §3's own done-when injects faults in-process only, and `plan-section-depends-on` declares no relation from s3 to s2, so a §3 node alone would close on an invariant that is still violated whenever a reader on another node recovers mid-move
